transcript:
Header: Date: 2025-04-15 Time: 16:00 UTC Duration: ~48 minutes Attendees: Alex Park (Redwood AE), Jamie Liu (Redwood SE), Priya Sharma (Stratus - Head of Search), Carlos Mendez (Stratus - ML Eng), Anya Petrov (Stratus - CTO)

Summary: Short discovery focused on embeddings/reranking architecture and vector DB integration. Main concerns: throughput for ~150 qps, index dimensionality, hybrid search with keyword+vector signals, and hosted vs dedicated latency/cost tradeoffs. Action items: share pricing/TCO, security docs, schedule benchmark.

Topics: embeddings model choice, vector DB options (Pinecone/Milvus/Weaviate), dimensionality (1536 vs 768), bulk upserts, hybrid search, reranking (sparse+dense pipelines), latency SLOs, dedicated capacity sizing, caching, and security controls (SOC2, KMS, VPC).

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex Park: Hi everyone, thanks for taking the time. Quick intro — I'm Alex, AE at Redwood, Jamie's my SE. How's everyone doing?
[00:07] Priya Sharma: Good thanks. We recently re-architected our search and looking at dense embeddings+rerank, so this call's to understand Redwood's hosted vs dedicated options, throughput, and how you'd integrate with our vector DB which is currently Pinecone.
[00:20] Jamie Liu: Awesome, thanks Priya. Can you tell us a bit about your traffic patterns? qps, batch vs real-time, offline index updates?
[00:27] Carlos Mendez: Sure — day peak about 150 QPS for search queries, mostly real-time. We do nightly re-indexes, plus nearline updates for new content; bulk upserts are ~10k vectors every few hours. Latency target for p95 is <150ms end-to-end for search+rerank.
[00:44] Alex Park: Got it. When you say end-to-end, does that include a neural rerank stage? and what's your current rerank model size / where is rerank hosted?
[00:52] Priya Sharma: Yes includes rerank. We do a cheap lexical recall with Elasticsearch, then dense recall from Pinecone, then a cross-encoder rerank in-house — currently CPU-based, but we'd like to move rerank to GPU to meet SLAs.
[01:07] Jamie Liu: Okay. A few clarifying q's: what's your embedding dimensionality and model? and are you open to using Redwood embeddings or bringing your own?
[01:14] Carlos Mendez: We're using 1536-d embeddings from an open model now (text-embedding-3-small-ish — excuse me names get fuzzy), but we might consider 768-d to save storage and speed up vector ops. We're evaluating quality tradeoffs.
[01:28] Alex Park: Good. On the hosting side, Redwood Hosted supports our embeddings and endpoints — you can either call Redwood to generate embeddings and then store in Pinecone, or you can host embeddings with Redwood Dedicated/Private and run rerank inside our runtime. For your throughput and latency, Dedicated usually gives predictable p95 because of reserved GPU capacity; Hosted can be fine but has more variability and may be more cost-efficient at lower QPS.
[01:52] Anya Petrov: Important for us: data residency and KMS integration — can you commit to customer-managed keys and VPC peering? We can't send raw content to third parties in a few regions.
[02:03] Jamie Liu: Yes, Redwood Private supports VPC/on-prem and KMS/HSM integrations; Dedicated also supports VPC peering and can be deployed in customer region. We'll follow up with SOC2 and KMS docs. (note: transcriber mis-heard 'KMS' as 'KMSs' earlier)
[02:20] Priya Sharma: On the vector DB side, we currently use Pinecone but are open to Milvus for cost reasons. How do you recommend integrating? Do you recommend plugging Redwood as an embedding generator that writes to Pinecone, or using Redwood as the reranker to read from Pinecone and score on GPU?
[02:35] Jamie Liu: Both are common. Pattern A: Redwood generate embeddings (lower latency) -> push to vector store -> do recall -> call Redwood rerank endpoint with top-K candidates for cross-encoder scoring. Pattern B: If you want the lowest e2e latency, run rerank inside Redwood Dedicated/Private and route retrieval results into the runtime via a proxied fetch — avoids extra network hop but requires hosting rerank in Redwood.
[02:57] Carlos Mendez: For 150 QPS, if we do a top-K rerank of 50 candidates per query, that's 7.5k inference calls per second if naive — that's not feasible. We were thinking batch rerank or candidate size 10-20. Thoughts?
[03:12] Jamie Liu: Right, naive cross-encoder scales badly. Two common approaches — limit K to 10-20, or use a dual-stage approach: cheap re-ranker (bi-encoder similarity or lightweight transformer) to narrow to 50 then cross-encoder for top 5. Also batching across queries and continuous batching in the runtime helps amortize GPU cost.
[03:30] Alex Park: Also worth considering MQ (multi-query) batching and using lower-dimensional embeddings for recall to speed up ANN, then use full model for rerank. And caching hot queries' rerank results can reduce QPS to the reranker significantly.
[03:45] Priya Sharma: What's your recommendation for dimensionality? 1536 vs 768? We worry about recall loss if we drop dims.
[03:52] Jamie Liu: It depends on model and latency/cost tradeoff. For many workloads, 768 dims (with a slightly larger model) maintains similar recall and halves storage and ANN distance computation. We can help run A/B comparisons. Redwood Optimize can recommend quantization and dimension profiles by workload.
[04:10] Anya Petrov: About throughput sizing — how do you size Dedicated for this? example numbers for GPUs and expected QPS for rerank.
[04:18] Jamie Liu: For cross-encoder BERT-large styles, a single A10/A100 instance can do X? (transcriber: numbers fuzzy) but practical approach is to do an initial benchmark with a representative dataset. Rough rule: for a GPU optimized cross-encoder with batching of 32, you might reach ~300-600 QPS for lightweight models; heavier models less. We'll propose a benchmark plan.
[04:38] Carlos Mendez: Are there any recommended vector DBs for hybrid search? We need lexical + vector recall.
[04:45] Alex Park: Elasticsearch (OpenSearch) + Pinecone is common: do a textual filter and then vector recall, or Milvus/Weaviate which support hybrid natively. Also consider using Redis vector or Qdrant. The key is to ensure the vector store can do filtered ANN and high-throughput upserts.
[05:00] Priya Sharma: Security — we need audit logs, SSO/SAML, RBAC and data deletion guarantees for compliance.
[05:07] Jamie Liu: Redwood's Private and Dedicated offerings include audit logs, SSO/SAML integrations, RBAC, and retention policies; we'll share SOC2 docs. For hosted, we have data retention controls and you can request logs; but for strict compliance Private is preferred.
[05:24] Alex Park: Cost question — what's the TCO difference between pushing embeddings from Redwood Hosted and running Dedicated? We need numbers.
[05:31] Jamie Liu: We'll send a TCO spreadsheet comparing per-token embedding cost + vector DB egress vs Dedicated amortized GPU cost + storage. As a quick note, if you have steady throughput and need low p95, Dedicated often becomes cheaper at scale.
[05:45] Priya Sharma: Any limitations on bulk upserts to Redwood or rate limits when pushing embeddings from Redwood Hosted to Pinecone?
[05:52] Jamie Liu: No hard limit on API throughput, but we recommend chunking uploads and using our bulk endpoints. For heavy upserts, Dedicated + direct VPC peering to your vector DB often gives best throughput.
[06:05] Carlos Mendez: For rerank models, support for quantization? 8-bit inference?
[06:10] Jamie Liu: Our runtime supports quantized kernels and int8 where appropriate; quality tradeoffs vary. Redwood Optimize can recommend quantization profiles.
[06:20] Priya Sharma: What are next steps from here?
[06:23] Alex Park: We'll share pricing/TCO, SOC2/KMS docs, and Jamie will propose a benchmark plan and tentative infra requirements. Can we schedule a 60-minute SE benchmark session next week? 
[06:34] Priya Sharma: Yes, next Wednesday works.
[06:36] Alex Park: Great — thanks everyone. We'll follow up with notes and action items.
[06:40] Carlos Mendez: Thanks all.

(Transcription notes: occasional mis-attributions and model names; speaker labels sometimes generic; timestamps approximate.)
